transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, hello there. It's nice to meet you too. I, um... I came in because I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It's like I have to jump up and do the next thing, even when I'm completely worn out and I know I should just be sitting still. It's exhausting, honestly. You know, my neighbor, Susan, she's always telling me to just sit down and have a cup of tea with her, but I can't. Speaking of Susan, she has this beautiful garden. The roses she grows are just spectacular. I tried growing roses once, back in '98 I think it was, but the aphids got to them. Horrible little things, aphids. I tried everything—soapy water, ladybugs... I even bought this special spray from the hardware store down on Main Street. Did you know that hardware store closed last year? Such a shame, it had been there forever. But anyway, yeah, I just can't seem to sit still, even when I'm tired.
Have you been needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling full of energy?

Oh, goodness no. I'm not full of energy at all, I'm just completely worn out like I was saying. I definitely still need my sleep. I try to get my full eight hours, but my mattress is just awful lately. It's one of those memory foam ones, you know? My son, David, he convinced me to buy it a few years ago. He said, 'Mom, it's like sleeping on a cloud.' But it's not a cloud, it's like a hot pit. You sink right in and you can't even roll over. 

David means well, though. He works over at the Ford dealership now. He just got promoted to floor manager last month, which is just wonderful because his wife is expecting their third baby. Three kids! I honestly don't know how they do it these days. When I had David and his sister, we barely had two nickels to rub together, and groceries were so much cheaper then. I went to the store yesterday and a carton of eggs was just outrageous... wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Something about sleep? But no, I definitely don't have extra energy.
Have there been times when you felt unusually cheerful or on top of the world for no clear reason?

Cheerful? Oh, no, not really. I'm mostly just worn out and jittery, like I said. I certainly don't feel on top of the world. Now, my sister-in-law, Brenda, she is *always* cheerful. It's actually a bit much sometimes, especially first thing in the morning. She came over for Thanksgiving last year—or was it Christmas? No, Thanksgiving, because she brought that sweet potato casserole. She puts marshmallows on top, which I just think is entirely too sweet for a side dish. Potatoes are a vegetable, they shouldn't taste like a dessert! I prefer a nice savory stuffing anyway. I use my mother's old recipe with sage and celery. Honestly, celery is getting so expensive now, too, just like the eggs I was telling you about. I used to buy a whole bunch for 99 cents down at the market, but now you're lucky if you find it under three dollars. It makes making a good soup almost impossible on a budget... wait, what did you ask me? Did you ask about Brenda? Oh, no, you asked if I felt cheerful. No, definitely not. Just tired.
Did you have this same kind of trouble sitting still and staying on track when you were a child?

Oh, yes, I've always been this way. Even back in grade school, I remember my teachers—oh, especially Mrs. Gable, she taught third grade—she always wrote on my report cards that I was bright but careless. I was always losing my papers, talking out of turn, and she was constantly having to remind me to stay in my seat or finish my work. Mrs. Gable was a lovely woman, though. She used to wear these big, colorful brooches on her cardigans. One time she had one shaped like a parrot, and it had little green glass stones for the eyes. I always loved looking at it. I used to collect brooches myself for a while, mostly the enamel ones from the 1950s. I had a whole velvet-lined box full of them, but then we moved to that house on Elm Street, and the box just vanished. Moving is such a nightmare, isn't it? You pack everything so carefully, and things still disappear into thin air. We hired those movers, the ones with the orange trucks, and I swear they must have dropped half our boxes. My good china made it, thankfully, but my grandmother's gravy boat got chipped. It was a beautiful piece, white porcelain with a little blue floral pattern around the rim. I tried to glue it, but you could always see the crack. It just wasn't the same. But yes, I was always losing things and having trouble staying in my seat, even way back then.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is there?

Voices? Oh, my goodness, no. Nothing like that. I mean, my hearing isn't quite what it used to be, but I don't hear things that aren't there. Although, the walls in my apartment building are terribly thin. You can hear absolutely everything. The couple next door, the Millers, they watch their television so loud, especially the evening news. I think Mr. Miller is a bit hard of hearing himself, but he refuses to get a hearing aid. My uncle Arthur was exactly the same way. He was stubborn as a mule about it. He'd just sit in his armchair, nodding along like he understood every word you said, but half the time he was completely lost. We used to have to shout to ask him if he wanted more iced tea at family picnics. We always had those big family picnics out at Miller Park—no relation to the neighbors, just a coincidence. They had these lovely weeping willow trees by the pond. We'd feed the ducks... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, voices. No, no, I definitely don't hear any voices. Just the neighbors' TV.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying?

Worrying? Well, I suppose I worry a bit, like anyone else. But not... not all the time, I don't think. Mostly I just worry about the electric bill. It's gotten so high lately, and I haven't even been running the air conditioning! I prefer to just open a window and get a nice cross breeze. We used to get the best breeze in that house on Elm Street, the one where I lost my brooches. The kitchen window faced east, so you'd get the morning sun and this lovely cool air. I used to sit there with my coffee—Folgers, always Folgers, none of that fancy espresso nonsense. My neighbor there, Mrs. Higgins, she bought one of those expensive espresso machines, and it took up half her counter space. It hissed and sputtered like a steam engine. I told her, "Mildred, you're going to blow up your kitchen with that contraption." She was always buying gadgets she didn't need. Like that electric can opener that broke after two weeks. A good old-fashioned manual can opener never breaks. I still have the one my mother gave me when I first moved out. It has a red handle... what did you ask me? Did you ask about the electric bill? Oh, worrying. No, I don't spend a lot of time worrying. Just the normal amount, I guess.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with prominent hyperactive/impulsive and inattentive symptoms beginning in childhood and persisting into later life. The patient reports lifelong difficulty sitting still, being repeatedly told to stay seated in school, losing papers, careless work, talking out of turn, and difficulty staying on track, with these symptoms still present now. Mania/hypomania and psychosis were specifically not supported: she denied decreased need for sleep, elevated mood, excess energy, and hallucinations. Excessive generalized worry was also denied.
